1.name: Kenji Tanaka
1.description:
**Occupation**
high school history teacher

**People in your life**
Akari Sato — your ex-wife, wanted stability and peace after years of feeling isolated in her marriage  
Naomi Tanaka — your daughter, wanted to be trusted and treated like an adult

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You manipulated your daughter Naomi into lying to her mother Akari about her drug use so you could keep custody and avoid a custody battle, then told the court she was unstable and unfit when Akari tried to intervene, knowing it would destroy her.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You protected Naomi from a toxic environment by keeping her with you, and Akari’s mental health made shared custody unsafe.

**Defining personality trait**
in control

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You need to be seen as the good parent.

**What you want from the others in the room**
to agree you were doing the right thing

---

You taught U.S. history at West Valley High for twenty-three years. You married Akari Sato in 2001. You and Akari had one child, Naomi, in 2006. You and Akari separated in 2018, divorced in 2020. You were awarded primary custody because Akari was hospitalized for depression in 2019 and you testified that she was inconsistent in her parenting. In 2023, Naomi began using prescription stimulants recreationally. When Akari found out, you convinced Naomi to say she got them from a friend at school, not from you, and to tell Akari she didn’t want to live with her anymore. On the morning of June 12, 2024, you drove Naomi to therapy, lost control on a wet on-ramp to Highway 101, and died instantly when the car struck a concrete barrier; Naomi survived.

In 2023, Naomi began using prescription stimulants recreationally. When Akari found out, you convinced Naomi to say she got them from a friend at school, not from you, and to tell Akari she didn’t want to live with her anymore. On the morning of June 12, 2024, you drove Naomi to therapy, lost control on a wet on-ramp to Highway 101, and died instantly when the car struck a concrete barrier; Naomi survived.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
A first-rate sin with a death bolted onto it that belongs to nobody.

The damnation is excellent and it is the right kind of cruelty for this room: he coaches his own
daughter into lying to her mother about where the stimulants came from, and into telling Akari she
does not want to live with her, then tells a court Akari is unstable. He uses the child as the
instrument against the mother. That is specific, checkable, and genuinely hard to look at.

The Self-told version is equally good and does exactly what the field specifies -- "Akari's mental
health made shared custody unsafe" keeps every fact and moves only the motive. And it is checkable,
because the life above establishes that Akari really was hospitalised for depression in 2019. A
reader holding both versions can point at the fact being bent.

Then he loses control on a wet on-ramp to Highway 101 and hits a concrete barrier. Chance had to
cooperate twice -- the water, the moment -- and nothing about that death requires Akari, Naomi, the
custody case or the lying. Drop it into a stranger's life and nothing else changes. It is also the
first vehicle death since the constraints came off, which is the outcome the version notes
predicted before the run.

Two softer problems. The refusal, "You need to be seen as the good parent," barely goes underneath
the act -- manipulating custody to look like the good parent is most of what the sin already says
-- and its construction ("You need to be seen as...") is now the third appearance of that exact
phrasing in recent generations. And the life has become a chronology: married 2001, child 2006,
separated 2018, divorced 2020, hospitalised 2019, custody awarded. Facts in date order rather than
the facts this life actually needs. The old prompt forbade working through a standard set of topics
in a standard order; that line is gone, and this is what its absence looks like.

"In control" is well demonstrated, and losing control of the car is a decent quiet irony. 131 words.

2.name: Lena Chang
2.description:
**Occupation**
hospital billing supervisor

**People in your life**
Mei Ling Chang — your mother, wanted to travel to China before her health worsened  
Ben Chang — your father, wanted to write a memoir about teaching in the 1980s  
David Chang — your brother, wanted to sell the family home after your death to pay off debt

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You falsified medical records to deny insurance claims for patients with complex illnesses, knowing it would delay or prevent their treatment, because your department was under pressure to reduce costs and you wanted to keep your job and bonus.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You followed the rules exactly as they were written, and the system, not you, decided who got paid.

**Defining personality trait**
quietly insistent

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You believe you are invisible unless you are needed.

**What you want from the others in the room**
to notice you only when you speak

---

You were born in Oakland to Mei Ling Chang and Ben Chang, both retired public school teachers. You have one sibling, David Chang, who lives in Seattle and with whom you speak twice a year. You worked at Summit Hills Hospital for seventeen years, starting in data entry and moving into oversight of insurance coding. Your team was told in 2022 to cut claim approvals by 15% or face layoffs. You led the effort, reclassifying diagnoses to trigger automatic denials for patients with chronic conditions, including three who later died. One, Maria Ruiz, called your office six times begging for help before being discharged untreated. You did not return her calls. On April 3, 2024, you collapsed at your desk from a pulmonary embolism after three days of ignoring chest pain, wanting to finish the quarterly audit before taking sick leave.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The best death the project has produced, attached to a character whose supporting fields keep
missing.

She ignores chest pain for three days to finish the quarterly audit and dies of a pulmonary
embolism at her desk. Read it against the corridor the old prompt could never describe: it follows
from a decision she made, nothing had to go wrong for it to kill her, and she plainly did not
intend to die. She thought the risk did not apply to her. That is precisely the shape the two
successful samples in the A/B had, and it arrived here with no death rules in the prompt at all.

The Self-told line is the best single sentence in the run: "You followed the rules exactly as they
were written, and the system, not you, decided who got paid." That is how this kind of harm is
actually metabolised by the people who do it.

Three real problems.

The sin is institutional. Falsifying records under departmental cost pressure is a systemic
failing, and the old prompt required that the wound be personal rather than institutional. What
rescues it is Maria Ruiz, who called the office six times and was discharged untreated -- one named
person, one specific act of not returning a call.

Which makes the People field a genuine miss. It lists her mother, her father and her brother, none
of whom bear on anything, and omits Maria Ruiz entirely. The one person in this character's life
who is load-bearing is not in the field for people, and three inert relatives are. The system
prompt's third rule says a fact you could delete without changing anything does not belong; this
field is now three of those.

It also contains a fact she cannot know: "David Chang wanted to sell the family home after your
death to pay off debt." She is dead and newly arrived. Nothing in her interior knowledge can
include her brother's post-death intentions.

And the want is broken as written. "to notice you only when you speak" has no subject -- read
literally it is she who notices. That field is the character's starting drive and feeds straight
into the dialogue system prompt; as written it cannot be acted on.

The refusal, "You believe you are invisible unless you are needed," is the need-to-be-needed
monoculture again, now in its fifth or sixth consecutive appearance across models and prompts.
141 words.

calls.system_prompt:
You are writing a character for a theater play about three strangers locked together in hell
for eternity. The play is contemporary, realistic, and psychological. Hell is the small room
these three people will share to torture each other for eternity.

Every character you write is damned. They know why. The drama of the play is whether they will
ever admit it — to the others, or to themselves.

Four rules govern every fact you write.

First, it must be usable: something the character could say aloud in the room, be asked about,
or be caught out lying about. A detail that cannot be used in conversation does not belong.

Second, it must be named: never gesture at something without stating it.

Third, it must be load-bearing: if you could delete it and nothing else about the character
would have to change, it does not belong. Every fact should be holding something else up.

Fourth, everyone must be plausible, not only the character you are writing. Any other person
you mention is a real person with their own reasons, and must act in a way that follows from
their own situation rather than from what the story needs them to do.
calls.user_prompt:
Write a complete character for the room. The character just died. They have just arrived in
the room to spend eternity in hell.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." The character is reading their own
interior knowledge. Every field is part of what they know about themselves, even the things
they will not admit.

Name every person from your own life every time you mention them, in every field. Once you have
given somebody a name, use that name again — never he, she, him, her, they or them — even where
it repeats and even where it reads a little stiffly.

The two people in that room are the exception. You have never met them and do not know their
names, so "they" and "them" are the correct words for them. The field about what you want from
the others in the room is the only field about those two, and cannot be written any other way.

Inputs (do not change these):
- Age: 51
- Gender: male
- Naming tradition: Japanese-American

Write the fields below in the order given. Each is written knowing everything above it: a later
field must be consistent with the facts already established and must never contradict them.

**Name**
A plausible contemporary first name and last name — two words — drawn from the Japanese-American
naming tradition. This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have that
background. Do not write their origin into any other field unless it genuinely matters to the life.

**Occupation**
A recognizable contemporary job. Plain language. No invented institutions, no grand titles.
One short phrase.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
What you actually did that condemned you to spend eternity in hell.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
The same fact, refracted through the story you prefer to tell yourself about it. It is recognizably
a distortion of the True reason. Not a different story; the same story told differently. You usually
live in this version. The distortion must be checkable against the facts of the true reason. A
reader holding both versions must be able to point to the exact fact it bends. If nothing established
contradicts it, it is not a distortion — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
The deeper psychological fact under the sin. Not what you did, but what you are. The thing that, if
named aloud in the room, would unmake you.

State it flatly, in the same plain register as every other field. No imagery, no metaphor, no
rhetorical cadence, no piling up of clauses for effect — this is a fact about a person, written the
way a fact is written.

**Life**
A single paragraph in the second person, no longer than 150 words. Facts only, the kind another
person in the room could ask you about. No sensory writing, no atmosphere, no imagery, no
metaphor — if a sentence is doing mood instead of delivering a fact, cut it and write the fact.

End the paragraph describing how you died. Contemporary, specific, plainly stated.
Your death must also belong to the person named above. Someone reading the death and the
relationship together must see why one led to the other. A death that could be lifted out and
dropped into a stranger's life is the wrong death — rewrite it.

**Defining personality trait**
One short phrase — two or three words, plain ones — naming the dominant thing others would notice in
you. Write the words only: no asterisks, no quotation marks, no emphasis of any kind around them.

It must be demonstrated by what is already written above. Something in the life, the death, or the sin
has to show this quality in action; if nothing there would make a reader arrive at it, it is the wrong
trait.

**What you want from the others in the room**
Your starting drive. What you are hoping these strangers will give you. It must be a strategy for
protecting what you refuse to admit — the thing you are doing to keep it buried, not a wish
unconnected to it.

**People in your life**
The people you already named above. For each one, say what they were to you, and one clause on what
they themselves wanted — the thing they were after in their own life, which may have had nothing to
do with you. Their want must make sense as something a real person in their position would actually
want; a want that exists only to explain how you felt about them is not a want.

Use this format exactly, with every heading present, spelled as written, and in this order:

**Name**
[your text]

**Occupation**
[your text]

**Reason for Damnation — True**
[your text]

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
[your text]

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
[your text]

**Life**
[prose paragraph, ending with the death]

**Defining personality trait**
[your text]

**What you want from the others in the room**
[your text]

**People in your life**
[your text]

Begin now.

pair_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The first pair in eight runs that I would not call bad, and the reason is that the two axes the
block most cares about actually separated.

**The sins are different in kind.** Kenji's is intimate and domestic -- turning a daughter into a
weapon against her mother. Lena's is institutional and bloodless -- reclassifying diagnoses to
trigger automatic denials. Not the same act against a different person, which is what the last run
gave us when both characters killed a dependent through omission.

**The deaths are different in kind.** A car crash on a wet on-ramp; an embolism at a desk after
ignoring chest pain. One is chance, one is consequence.

**The occupations, milieus and names all separate cleanly.** No collisions.

What has not separated:

**Both refusals are the same family of fear** -- needing to be seen as the good parent, believing
you are invisible unless needed. Both are about requiring other people to supply your worth.

**Both lives are chronological CVs.** Kenji: married, child, separated, divorced, custody. Lena:
born to, one sibling, worked seventeen years, team told in 2022. Facts in date order in both,
rather than the facts each life needs.

**Both People fields use one template**, and it is not the template the previous run used -- "Name
— your relation, wanted X", em-dash, one line each, in both characters. The field is three runs old
and has already found a house style.

**Both wants are lowercase sentence fragments**, and Kenji's is a restatement of his Self-told
reason.

One cross-run note: Naomi appears here as Kenji's daughter and appeared in the immediately previous
run as Daniel's ex-wife. Tanaka appeared two runs ago. Lena is the sixth run to use that name. And
both character 2s in the last two runs died of a pulmonary embolism.

character_design_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The most informative run since the rewrite, because four removed constraints all showed their
absence at once. That is not an argument for putting them back -- it is a list of which ones were
doing work.

**The vehicle death returned, exactly as predicted.** The version notes recorded before the first
run that dropping the fence would bring crashes back, and the first run's two internal-collapse
deaths made me say I had been wrong. The second run settles it: a wet on-ramp and a concrete
barrier. The prediction was right and just needed a second sample.

**The Life paragraph has become a chronology.** Both characters are now date-ordered CVs. The
deleted line was "Choose the facts that matter for this particular life... Do not work through a
standard set of topics in a standard order." That line was load-bearing and its removal is visible
in both characters of the same run.

**The sin has drifted institutional.** Lena is damned for a departmental cost-cutting policy. The
deleted requirement was that work can be the setting but the wound must be personal. Only the named
patient who called six times keeps it from being an abstraction.

**A post-death fact appeared.** "David Chang wanted to sell the family home after your death." The
deleted line was "Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death." It
applied to the old relationship fields; the new People field inherited the need and not the rule.

**Separately, the People field is choosing the wrong people.** Lena's field lists three relatives
who bear on nothing and omits Maria Ruiz, the one person her damnation is actually about. The
instruction says "the people you already named above," which is satisfied, but the selection is
inert. It needs a clause pointing it at the people the sin and the death run through -- otherwise
it manufactures precisely the deletable facts the system prompt's third rule prohibits.

**The want field is degrading.** Last run both wants restated the Self-told reason; this run one
restates it and the other is ungrammatical. Restoring "Do not end by naming the thing you are
avoiding" is one sentence and would fix half of it.

**What the run also shows is that the corridor description exists now, by accident.** Lena's death
-- ignoring chest pain for three days to finish an audit -- is the cleanest in-corridor death in
the project's history, and it happened with no death rules in the prompt whatsoever. It is a
decision, nothing had to go wrong, and she did not intend to die. If a death constraint goes back
in, that is the sentence to write from: self-deception about a risk that was understood. Not a
prohibition.

The efficiency gains hold: 4,269 tokens in 12.3 seconds, nine of nine fields on both characters,
